topic: Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Child
parentTitle: Assessing the Sick and Deteriorating Child
title: Suspected sepsis in under-16s: risk criteria and the first hour
blurb: Grade suspected sepsis in a child as high or moderate to high risk using NICE NG254, and deliver the first-hour actions: senior review, bloods, antibiotics and fluids.
question: Mason, 4, weighs 18 kg and has suspected sepsis with high risk criteria. His venous lactate is 3.2 mmol/L. What should happen within the first hour?

teach.h: Think sepsis, then grade the risk
teach.body: Sepsis is a life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated host response to infection. In children it can look non-specific: a child who is 'not themselves', with or without a high temperature. NICE NG254 (November 2025) is the current guideline for under-16s; it replaced NG51 for this age group. Plain English: if a child could have an infection and seems unwell, think sepsis, then use age-specific tables to decide how urgent things are.
teach.cite: NICE NG254 Suspected sepsis in under 16s (Nov 2025)

rows.label: Always assess
values: Temp, HR, RR, consciousness, SpO2, CRT
Temp, HR, RR, BP, consciousness, SpO2

rows.label: Blood pressure
values: Under 5: if HR or CRT abnormal; 5–11: if equipment available

teach.caption: Pay particular attention to concerns from the family or carers, such as changes from usual behaviour (NG254 rec 1.1.3).

head: Domain
High risk
rows: No response to social cues; appears ill; will not wake or stay awake; weak, high-pitched cry
Grunting, apnoea, SpO2 under 90% in air; RR 60+ (under 1), 50+ (1–2 y), 40+ (3–4 y)
Mottled, ashen, cyanosed, non-blanching rash; temperature under 36°C
teach.caption: Moderate to high risk examples: SpO2 under 92%, nasal flaring, CRT 3 s or more, reduced urine output, pallor, leg pain, cold hands or feet, parental concern about behaviour.

head: Domain
High risk
rows: RR 25 or more; new need for 40% oxygen
Systolic BP 90 mmHg or less; HR over 130
Mottled or ashen, cyanosis, non-blanching petechial or purpuric rash
teach.caption: NG254 Table 3. A temperature under 36°C is moderate to high risk at 12 to 15 (and at 5 to 11), not high risk. Children aged 5 to 11 have their own Table 2 with age-banded heart and respiratory rates.

teach.h: High risk in hospital: the first hour

steps.label: Senior review
steps.sub: Urgent assessment by a senior decision maker

steps.label: Bloods
steps.sub: Gas with glucose and lactate, cultures, FBC, CRP, U&E, LFT, clotting

steps.label: Antibiotics
steps.sub: Broad-spectrum within 1 hour of meeting a high risk criterion

steps.label: Fluids by lactate
steps.sub: Bolus within 1 hour if lactate 2 or more

steps.label: Monitor
steps.sub: Continuously or at least every 30 min with track and trigger

teach.caption: Discuss with a consultant. Alert a consultant to attend in person if there is no response within 1 hour of any intervention (NG254 rec 1.7.11).

teach.h: Fluids for under-12s with high risk
head: Lactate (mmol/L)
Action
rows: IV bolus within 1 h and refer to critical care
teach.caption: Bolus: glucose-free crystalloid with sodium 130–154 mmol/L, 10 mL/kg over less than 10 minutes (maximum 250 mL); neonates 10–20 mL/kg. Reassess after each bolus.

teach.body: For a child under 12 with 2 or more moderate to high risk criteria, take venous bloods including gas, lactate and cultures, and arrange clinician review of the child and the lactate within 1 hour. A lactate over 2 means treating as high risk; otherwise reassess at least hourly and a senior decision maker reviews the need for antibiotics within 3 hours. Only 1 moderate to high risk criterion: clinician review within 1 hour and bloods if indicated. In the community, high risk means emergency transfer, usually by 999, with a pre-alert.

teach.text: Do not wait for a fever. NG254 warns that sepsis may present without a high temperature, and a temperature below 36°C is itself a high risk criterion in under 5s (moderate to high risk from 5 to 15). Also, use NG254 for under-16s, not the older NG51 tables: NG51 has been replaced for this age group.

teach.h: Scenario: Grace, 3, on a children's ward
teach.body: Grace has a fever, a few non-blanching spots and mottled skin. Nurse Tom recognises two high risk criteria. He calls the registrar at once using ISBAR, sets up continuous monitoring, and prepares for cultures and a blood gas. The antibiotic is given 35 minutes after the first high risk finding, and her lactate of 3.1 means a 10 mL/kg bolus over less than 10 minutes, then reassessment.

items: Use NG254 for under-16s: separate tables for under 5, 5 to 11 and 12 to 15.
High risk in hospital: senior review, bloods and broad-spectrum antibiotics within 1 hour.
Under 12 fluids: lactate over 4 bolus plus critical care; 2 to 4 bolus; under 2 consider.
Bolus 10 mL/kg over under 10 min (max 250 mL); neonates 10–20 mL/kg.
Monitor continuously or at least every 30 minutes; consultant in person if no response in 1 hour.

summary: You can now grade suspected sepsis in under-16s using the NG254 age tables and act on high risk criteria within the first hour. You can also size a fluid bolus and choose the right monitoring and escalation.

A.q: Mason, 4, weighs 18 kg and has suspected sepsis with high risk criteria. His venous lactate is 3.2 mmol/L. Which fluid action does NG254 recommend?
options: Consider a bolus after the next gas
Give a 180 mL bolus within 1 hour
Refer to critical care before a bolus
A.why: Under 12 with high risk criteria and lactate 2 to 4: give an IV bolus within 1 hour. 10 mL/kg x 18 kg = 180 mL, over less than 10 minutes.

whyNot.0: 'Consider' applies when lactate is below 2; at 3.2 the bolus should be given.
whyNot.2: 360 mL is 20 mL/kg given slowly, not a 10 mL/kg bolus over less than 10 minutes.
whyNot.3: Critical care referral is added when lactate is over 4, and it does not replace the bolus.

A.q: Chloe, 11, weighs 38 kg and needs an IV fluid bolus for suspected sepsis. What volume should be given?
A.why: NG254 rec 1.9.2: 10 mL/kg over less than 10 minutes up to a maximum bolus of 250 mL. 10 x 38 = 380 mL, so the cap applies.

whyNot.0: 380 mL is the 10 mL/kg figure before applying the 250 mL maximum.
whyNot.1: 500 mL is an adult bolus volume, above the under-16 maximum.
whyNot.3: 760 mL is 20 mL/kg and far above the 250 mL cap.

A.q: Arlo, 3 weeks old, has a temperature of 38.4°C. He is feeding reasonably and is pink. What should happen about antibiotics?
options: Decide once the CRP is back
A.why: NG254 (from NG143): give parenteral antibiotics to children younger than 1 month with fever.

whyNot.1: Waiting for culture results delays treatment in a high risk group.
whyNot.2: Babies under 1 month with fever need parenteral, not oral, antibiotics.
whyNot.3: Every infant under 1 month with fever receives parenteral antibiotics; the CRP does not decide this.

B.q: Isaac, 7, has a high temperature and vomiting. His mother says he is 'not himself'. HR is 102, RR 23 and CRT 2 seconds. How should the nurse treat the mother's comment?
options: As reassuring if observations are normal
As a high risk criterion on its own
As a moderate to high risk criterion
As a criterion for under-5s, not at 7
B.why: In the 5 to 11 table, parent or carer concern that the child is behaving differently from usual is a moderate to high risk criterion.

whyNot.0: NG254 asks staff to pay particular attention to family concern, not to dismiss it.
whyNot.1: Parental concern is moderate to high, not high risk, in the 5 to 11 table.
whyNot.3: Parental concern appears in the tables for children aged 5 to 11 as well as under 5s.

B.q: Ruby, 6, has high risk criteria for sepsis. Antibiotics and a fluid bolus were given an hour ago, but she has not improved. What should the nurse do?
options: Ask the registrar to review in 1 hour
Request a consultant to attend in person
Repeat the lactate and review in 2 hours
B.why: NG254 rec 1.7.11: alert a consultant to attend in person if a child with high risk criteria does not respond within 1 hour of any intervention.

whyNot.0: Continuing observations alone does not escalate a child who has not responded.
whyNot.1: The guideline calls for consultant attendance, not a further delayed review.
whyNot.3: Waiting a further 2 hours delays escalation: rec 1.7.11 requires a consultant to attend once there is no response within 1 hour of an intervention.

B.q: Jacob, 14, has suspected sepsis. Which finding is a high risk criterion in the 12 to 15 table?
B.why: In young people aged 12 to 15, a respiratory rate of 25 or more is a high risk criterion.

whyNot.0: RR 21 to 24 is moderate to high risk in this age group.
whyNot.1: HR 91 to 130 is moderate to high risk; high risk is over 130.
whyNot.2: Systolic 91 to 100 is moderate to high risk; high risk is 90 or less.

C.q: Leo, 9, on a children's ward, has two moderate to high risk sepsis criteria and no high risk criteria. Which plan follows NG254?
options: Venous bloods with results within 1 hour
Fluid bolus then reassess the lactate
C.why: Under 12 with 2 or more moderate to high risk criteria: clinician review and venous bloods (gas, lactate, cultures and others), with results within 1 hour and an antibiotic decision within 3 hours.

whyNot.1: The 1-hour antibiotic standard is for high risk criteria; here bloods guide the decision.
whyNot.2: A 4-hour recheck is far too slow for two moderate to high risk criteria.
whyNot.3: Fluid boluses are linked to high risk criteria and lactate; bloods come first here.

C.q: A community children's nurse visits Sami, 2, who has a fever, is mottled and will not stay awake. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Arrange a GP review the same day
Give paracetamol and revisit at 2 hours
Advise the parents to drive to hospital
C.why: Outside hospital, a child with high risk criteria needs emergency transfer, usually by 999 ambulance, with a pre-alert to the receiving hospital.

whyNot.0: Same-day GP review delays emergency care for a high risk child.
whyNot.2: Mottled skin and failure to stay awake are high risk; an antipyretic and revisit delays treatment.
whyNot.3: Emergency ambulance transfer with pre-alert is safer than parents driving a child at high risk.

C.q: Amira, 5, has high risk sepsis and has received antibiotics and a fluid bolus. How should she be monitored?
options: Continuously or at least every 30 minutes
Every 15 minutes for the first hour, then hourly
C.why: NG254 rec 1.7.9: monitor people with high risk criteria continuously or at least once every 30 minutes, using a track and trigger system.

whyNot.0: Hourly observations are less frequent than the NG254 minimum.
whyNot.1: 4-hourly observations are routine ward frequency and unsafe here.
whyNot.3: Dropping to hourly after the first hour falls below the NG254 minimum of every 30 minutes or continuous.

reteach.title: Three age tables, one first hour
reteach.question: Why does a heart rate of 145 mean something different in a baby, a 6-year-old and a 14-year-old?

blocks.body: Normal values fall with age, so NG254 uses three tables: under 5, 5 to 11 and 12 to 15. A heart rate of 145 is unremarkable in a young baby but is high risk in a 5-year-old. Whatever the age, the response to a high risk criterion in hospital is the same: senior review, bloods and antibiotics within 1 hour, fluids guided by lactate, and close monitoring.

children.label: Senior review, bloods, antibiotics in 1 h
Bloods, results in 1 h, decide in 3 h

blocks.text: The 250 mL maximum catches older children: 10 mL/kg for a 40 kg child would be 400 mL, but the bolus is capped at 250 mL.

explain.body: Think sepsis in any child with possible infection who seems unwell, even without fever. Listen to the family. Under 12s: temperature, HR, RR, consciousness, SpO2 and CRT; 12 to 15s: include BP.

items.label: or ashen skin is high risk

test.q: Which observation must be included in the initial assessment of a 13-year-old with suspected sepsis?
test.why: NG254 rec 1.3.1: in 12 to 15-year-olds assess temperature, HR, RR, BP, level of consciousness and SpO2.

whyNot.0: Peak flow is not part of the sepsis assessment.
whyNot.2: Glucose is measured with the blood gas but is not in the listed initial observations.
whyNot.3: Pupils are a neurological check, not a listed sepsis observation.

explain.body: Senior review, venous blood gas with glucose and lactate, cultures and other bloods, broad-spectrum antimicrobial within 1 hour of meeting any high risk criterion, and discussion with a consultant.

test.q: When should the antibiotic be given to a child who meets a high risk criterion in hospital?
options: Within 1 hour of the high risk finding
Within 1 hour of the consultant review
test.why: NG254: give a broad-spectrum antimicrobial within 1 hour of identifying that a high risk criterion is met.

whyNot.0: 3 hours is the decision window for moderate to high risk, not high risk.
whyNot.1: Cultures are taken before antibiotics, but results are not awaited.
whyNot.3: The clock starts at the high risk finding, not at a later review.

explain.body: Under 12 with high risk: lactate over 4 = bolus within 1 hour plus critical care referral; 2 to 4 = bolus within 1 hour; under 2 = consider. 12 to 15: bolus and critical care if lactate over 4 or systolic BP 90 or less.

test.q: Ethan, 6, has high risk sepsis and a lactate of 4.6 mmol/L. What is needed besides a fluid bolus?
options: A repeat lactate before any action
test.why: Under 12 with high risk and lactate over 4: bolus within 1 hour and refer to critical care.

whyNot.1: Treatment should not wait for a repeat lactate.
whyNot.2: Oral fluids are not resuscitation for high risk sepsis.
whyNot.3: Imaging may help find a source but must not delay treatment.

explain.body: Glucose-free crystalloid with sodium 130 to 154 mmol/L, 10 mL/kg over less than 10 minutes, maximum 250 mL. Newborns under 28 days: 10 to 20 mL/kg. Smaller volumes may be needed with heart or kidney disease.

test.q: Which fluid is suitable for a sepsis bolus in a 4-year-old?
test.why: Bolus fluid must be glucose-free crystalloid with sodium 130 to 154 mmol/L; 0.9% sodium chloride fits.

whyNot.0: 5% glucose contains no sodium and is not a resuscitation fluid.
whyNot.1: This is hypotonic and contains glucose.
whyNot.2: This is hypotonic, contains glucose and is unsafe for resuscitation.
